say.text: Your registrar says 'FNAC first, it is the gold standard'. You have a euthyroid adult with a solitary nodule.
Before any needle, what is the first step?

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNAC straight away, to get the answer
Serum TSH and neck ultrasound, then decide on FNAC
Radioiodine scan first, to split hot from cold nodules
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Needle-first feels decisive, and FNAC is the test that settles what a nodule is.
But the needle is not the first step. The cheap first work-up comes before it, and FNAC is asked for once that work-up points to it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: blood and imaging come first, the needle after.

say.text: That choice is not right. A scan does sort hot from cold nodules, so it sounds like a sensible first look.
But a scan is done only when TSH is low, to find a hot nodule. With a normal TSH it adds nothing to the first step.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the trigger: a low TSH is what sends you to a scan.

say.text: Right. Every nodule gets serum TSH and neck ultrasound first.
FNAC is the test of choice for the nature of the nodule, and a scan follows only when TSH is low.
Think about what every nodule gets first, before any imaging or needle. Then ask what a scan is for.
A Bethesda IV report is back: a follicular neoplasm.
Which finding would make the pathologist call it follicular carcinoma?

choices.label: Nuclear grooves and ground-glass nuclei on the FNAC slide
Frozen section showing follicular architecture with atypia
Capsular or vascular invasion on the resected lobe
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Nuclear detail is what cytologists read, so the diagnosis feels like it should be on the slide.
But grooves and ground-glass nuclei are papillary features, and FNAC cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: a needle sample shows cells, not whether a capsule or vessel has been crossed.

say.text: That choice is not right. A frozen section is a quick look at architecture, so an early answer seems possible.
But frozen section is of little value for follicular lesions, and architecture cannot show invasion. Histology of the resected lobe decides.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that a quick section cannot settle invasion; the resected lobe does.

say.text: Right. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed on histology, by capsular or vascular invasion.
Cytology cannot make the diagnosis, and a frozen section of a follicular lesion is of little value.
Ask which tissue can show whether a capsule or a blood vessel has been crossed, and whether a needle or a quick section can see that.
A thyroid report mentions psammoma bodies, but it says nothing about the nuclei.
What can you conclude?

choices.label: Not enough alone, since they are supportive features
Papillary carcinoma, since psammoma bodies are specific to it
Papillary carcinoma, since the calcifications mark papillae
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Psammoma bodies are a classic papillary finding, so they feel like a signature.
But they also appear in serous ovarian tumours, meningioma and mesothelioma. They support the diagnosis; they do not make it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the calcifications are: a supportive sign, not an identity.

say.text: That choice is not right. Calcifications and papillae often turn up in the same report, so they seem linked.
But psammoma bodies are not the papillae, and the diagnosis rests on nuclear features. Architecture is supportive too.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that the papillary label is set by the nuclei, even when the calcifications are striking.

say.text: Right. Psammoma bodies support papillary carcinoma, but the call rests on nuclear features.
Without a nuclear description the report cannot make the diagnosis, whatever the calcifications show.
Ask what a report must describe before it can call a lesion papillary, and whether psammoma bodies are that description.
A registry lists every differentiated thyroid cancer seen over ten years, across all ages and districts.
Which type heads the list?

choices.label: Follicular carcinoma, the leader in iodine-poor hill areas
Papillary carcinoma, the leader in most registries
Follicular carcinoma, the leader in most registries
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Follicular cancer is the one that rises as iodine becomes scarce, so the hill-area idea feels decisive.
But that is a share within one setting. This registry covers every district, and the whole-list leader is a different histology.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the qualifier: follicular rises in share where iodine is scarce, not across the whole list.

say.text: That choice is not right. Follicular is a frequent histology, so it can look like the leader in a general list.
But the overall lead belongs to a different histology. Follicular is relatively more common only in iodine deficiency.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the overall leader first, then ask which setting changes it.

say.text: Right. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer overall, about 80–85% of cases.
Follicular carcinoma gains relative share only where iodine is scarce, so it does not head an all-district list.
Ask which histology is the most frequent across all ages and all districts. Then ask which setting changes the share.
Since 2016, one lesion was taken off the cancer list.
Which name replaces it?

choices.label: Encapsulated follicular variant of papillary carcinoma
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Exam keys taught this name for years, so it still sounds like the current label.
But it is the retired name. Non-invasive encapsulated tumours with papillary-like nuclei are no longer called carcinoma.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word carcinoma: under the change, this lesion was taken out of it.

say.text: That choice is not right. Encapsulation looks reassuring, but the word carcinoma makes it sound malignant.
But with no capsular or vascular invasion the lesion is not malignant under current classification. Invasion decides.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that encapsulation alone is not invasion.

say.text: Right. NIFTP is the non-invasive follicular neoplasm with papillary-like nuclei, which replaced the encapsulated follicular variant.
It is not a carcinoma, so the cancer pathway does not apply.
Ask what decides malignancy in these follicular tumours. Then ask whether this one shows that feature.
A 48-year-old woman has differentiated thyroid cancer that has spread to distant sites.
Which AJCC 8th edition stage applies?

choices.label: Stage IVB, since she is over the 45-year cut-off
Stage III, since she is over the 45-year cut-off
Stage II, since distant spread under 55 is stage II
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. The 45-year cut-off is the one older keys taught, so it feels current and familiar.
But the 8th edition moved the age cut-off to 55. A patient under that age is staged on its own two-stage scheme.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the cut-off year first, then read the stage.

say.text: That choice is not right. Distant spread feels like it should push the stage up, so stage III sounds plausible.
But for patients under 55 the 8th edition has only stage I and stage II, and distant spread sits within stage II.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that below the cut-off, distant spread does not take the stage above II.

say.text: Right. The 8th edition uses 55 as the cut-off, and under 55 there are only two stages.
Stage I is without distant spread and stage II is with it, so this patient is stage II.
Ask which age cut-off the current edition uses, and whether this patient falls on each side of it.
No hints from here on. Each of these is a cold check.
A firm lateral neck node is biopsied. The cells show papillary nuclei, and no thyroid primary is seen on examination.
What is it most likely?

choices.label: Benign ectopic thyroid tissue in the lateral neck
Blood-borne deposit from a papillary thyroid primary
Nodal metastasis of follicular carcinoma, its usual pattern
Nodal metastasis of papillary carcinoma, primary maybe occult

say.text: That choice is not right. 'Aberrant thyroid' sounds like a harmless remnant, which is why it tempts.
But a lateral node with papillary nuclei is a nodal metastasis, not normal tissue. The so-called lateral aberrant thyroid is a metastasis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the nuclei: a node that carries them is a deposit of cancer.

say.text: That choice is not right. Papillary cancer can reach the bloodstream, so a distant deposit sounds plausible.
But papillary carcinoma spreads mainly by lymphatics to the neck nodes. Blood spread is the follicular pattern.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so route first: papillary goes through lymphatics, and follicular goes through blood.

say.text: That choice is not right. Neck nodes are the first thing examined in any thyroid cancer, so they feel typical.
But nodal spread is uncommon in follicular carcinoma, and the papillary nuclei point to the papillary type.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that follicular cancer leans on the blood route more than the nodes.

say.text: Right. Papillary carcinoma spreads to the neck nodes, and a node with papillary nuclei is a metastasis.
The primary may not be palpable, so the node can be the first sign.
Four report-and-action pairs for thyroid cytology are offered.
Which one is correct?

choices.label: Bethesda II: surgery, since a benign nodule may still grow
Bethesda II: ultrasound follow-up, and surgery for pressure symptoms
Bethesda IV: cancer surgery, the same as for category V
Bethesda V: diagnostic lobectomy, the same as for IV

say.text: That choice is not right. A nodule that may grow sounds like a reason to remove it, so surgery feels cautious.
But a benign cytology report is managed by clinical and ultrasound follow-up. Surgery is for compression or cosmesis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the report from the nodule: benign means follow-up unless the nodule causes trouble.

say.text: That choice is not right. Both IV and V are not benign, so they feel like one group that needs the same plan.
But IV is a follicular neoplasm, managed first by diagnostic lobectomy or molecular testing. Cancer surgery belongs to V and VI.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that IV and V sit in different action boxes.

say.text: That choice is not right. Category V is suspicious, and a lobectomy is the diagnostic step for IV, so the two get blurred.
But V is managed as thyroid cancer, while diagnostic lobectomy belongs to IV. The two categories do not share an action.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the category and the action together for every Bethesda report.

say.text: Right. Bethesda II is benign, so it gets ultrasound and clinical follow-up.
Surgery is reserved for compression or cosmesis, and Bethesda IV and V take different actions.
A 2.5 cm unifocal papillary carcinoma is found. It is intrathyroidal, with no nodes and no radiation history.
Which extent of surgery fits current guidance?

choices.label: Total thyroidectomy, since every DTC is treated that way
Total thyroidectomy, the classic answer for any thyroid cancer
Lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, both acceptable under current guidance

say.text: That choice is not right. Total thyroidectomy is the big standard operation, so it feels like the safe default for every cancer.
But the classic answer was total thyroidectomy for DTC; current ATA guidance is not a single operation for every size and risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the size band: low-risk, unifocal, 1–4 cm, intrathyroidal.

say.text: That choice is not right. The classic key is total thyroidectomy, so the old answer feels like the right one.
But that is the old key. The size, nodes and risk decide the extent here, and the classic answer is not the rule for this tumour.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the risk group before you choose the operation.

say.text: Right. For a low-risk unifocal tumour of 1–4 cm with no nodes, lobectomy or total thyroidectomy are both acceptable.
The old key said total thyroidectomy for DTC; current guidance accepts the smaller operation here.
A patient with a low-risk papillary cancer has had total thyroidectomy. Radioiodine is being planned.
Which plan is right?

choices.label: No routine radioiodine, and TSH held at low-normal
Radioiodine for every patient, as standard after surgery
Drive TSH down to suppression before giving the dose
Keep TSH suppressed on levothyroxine during the dose

say.text: That choice is not right. Radioiodine is a powerful treatment, so giving it to everyone feels thorough.
But it is not given routinely to low-risk disease. The risk category decides who needs it, not the surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that the risk category, not the operation, decides the dose.

say.text: That choice is not right. Suppressed TSH is the long-term aim, so it feels like the right state for the dose too.
But suppression is the later goal and is matched to risk. Radioiodine uptake depends on TSH being high on the day of any dose.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the long-term target from the TSH state on the day of the dose.

say.text: That choice is not right. Keeping levothyroxine going feels like the safe continuation after surgery.
But levothyroxine is for replacement and long-term suppression. It does not make radioiodine uptake work on the day of a dose.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the long-term drug from the TSH needed on the day of the dose.

say.text: Right. Radioiodine is not given routinely to ATA low-risk disease, and TSH is held in the low-normal range.
Suppression is matched to risk: deeper for high-risk disease, low-normal for low-risk.
Which result after total thyroidectomy for papillary cancer would reassure you enough to stop the recurrence work-up?

choices.label: Undetectable thyroglobulin, although antibodies are raised
Rising thyroglobulin, though the iodine scan is negative
Undetectable thyroglobulin, no antibodies, clear neck ultrasound
Normal calcitonin, the marker that tracks papillary cancer

say.text: That choice is not right. An undetectable value looks like the end of the story, so it feels reassuring.
But antibodies make the thyroglobulin assay unreliable, so an undetectable value cannot be trusted alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the assay before you read the number.

say.text: That choice is not right. A negative iodine scan sounds like a clean result, so a rising value seems explained.
But the scan finds only iodine-avid disease. A rising thyroglobulin with a blank scan needs a further test, not reassurance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that a negative scan does not cancel a rising marker.

say.text: That choice is not right. Calcitonin is a tumour marker, so a normal value feels like a clean bill of health.
But calcitonin marks medullary carcinoma, not differentiated cancer. Papillary and follicular follow-up uses thyroglobulin.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note which marker belongs to which cancer.

say.text: Right. Thyroglobulin is the marker, and it is read only when antibodies are absent.
A clear neck ultrasound adds the imaging check for locoregional recurrence.
Which statement about complications after total thyroidectomy is correct?

choices.label: Nerve injury is the commonest problem, with bleeding close behind
Loss of a high-pitched voice means recurrent laryngeal palsy
A tense neck swelling is first treated by reintubation
Hypocalcaemia is the commonest, though nerve injury is feared most

say.text: That choice is not right. Nerve injury is the complication everyone fears, so it feels like the common one too.
But feared and frequent are different questions. Nerve palsy is serious, and it is not the commonest problem.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the feared complication from the frequent one.

say.text: That choice is not right. The voice change is real, and the recurrent nerve is the famous one, so it sounds linked.
But loss of high pitch and voice fatigue come from the cricothyroid muscle, supplied by a different branch. The recurrent nerve gives hoarseness.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the symptom to the muscle, then to the nerve.

say.text: That choice is not right. Reintubation is the airway reflex, so it feels like the first move for any noisy breathing.
But a tense neck swelling is a clot to release first, at the bedside. Airway steps come after the wound is opened.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the sequence matters: release the clot, then secure the airway.

say.text: Right. Transient hypocalcaemia is the commonest complication, from parathyroid hypofunction.
Nerve injury is the one to fear most; it is not the most common complication.

cards.q: What are the first tests for a solitary thyroid nodule, and what does FNAC answer?
cards.a: Serum TSH and neck ultrasound come first. Ultrasound-guided FNAC is the test of choice for the nature of the nodule; a scan follows only if TSH is low.

cards.q: How is papillary carcinoma diagnosed, and how is follicular carcinoma diagnosed?
cards.a: Papillary: nuclear features (optically clear nuclei, grooves, pseudoinclusions). Follicular: capsular or vascular invasion on histology; FNAC cannot do it.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer is most common overall, and which rises in iodine deficiency?
cards.a: Papillary carcinoma overall, about 80–85%. Follicular carcinoma rises in relative share in iodine-deficient areas.

cards.q: Usual route and sites of spread of papillary versus follicular carcinoma?
cards.a: Papillary spreads by lymphatics to neck nodes. Follicular spreads by blood to lung and bone, with nodes uncommon.

cards.q: Action for Bethesda II and for Bethesda IV?
cards.a: Bethesda II: clinical and ultrasound follow-up, surgery only for compression or cosmesis. Bethesda IV: diagnostic lobectomy or molecular testing.

cards.q: Extent of surgery for a low-risk DTC of 1–4 cm?
cards.a: Lobectomy or total thyroidectomy are both acceptable under ATA 2015; the PYQ key expected total thyroidectomy.

cards.q: When is radioiodine given, and what TSH is needed before a dose?
cards.a: Not routinely for ATA low-risk disease; recommended for high-risk and metastatic disease. A dose needs a high TSH, from withdrawal or recombinant TSH.

cards.q: Which marker follows DTC after total thyroidectomy, and what must be checked with it?
cards.a: Serum thyroglobulin, read only with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies negative and alongside neck ultrasound. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma.

cards.q: Commonest complication after total thyroidectomy, and first step for a tense neck haematoma?
cards.a: Transient hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypofunction. A tense neck haematoma: open the wound at the bedside first, then secure the airway.
